title: Newton's laws, weight and friction
blurb: Apply Newton's three laws, use F = ma with the net force, separate mass from weight, and calculate friction from the normal force.
question: A physical therapist assistant pushes a 50 kg linen cart with 150 N, and kinetic friction is 100 N. What is the cart's acceleration, why did it take more force to get it moving, and what would it weigh on the Moon?

teach.body: Formally, Newton's first law states that an object stays at rest, or keeps moving in a straight line at constant speed, unless a net (unbalanced) force acts on it. In plain English: things keep doing what they are doing until something pushes or pulls them unevenly. This resistance to a change in motion is inertia, and mass is its measure. A passenger lurching forward when a bus brakes, and the seat belt that stops her, both show it.

teach.caption: Balanced forces (net force zero) mean rest OR constant velocity. Unbalanced forces mean acceleration.

teach.body: The net force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration, and the acceleration points the same way as the net force. One newton (N) = 1 kg·m/s². Double the net force and the acceleration doubles; double the mass and it halves. Always use the NET force: subtract opposing forces such as friction first. Weight is a special case: W = mg, the gravitational force on a mass m.

items: A 1,200 kg car accelerates at 2.5 m/s²: F_net = 1,200 × 2.5 = 3,000 N.
A 10 kg box is pushed with 50 N against 20 N of friction: F_net = 30 N, so a = 30 ÷ 10 = 3.0 m/s².
The same net force acts on 2 kg and 6 kg carts: the 2 kg cart's acceleration is 3 times larger.
A 20 kg crate on a level floor (g = 10 m/s²): normal force = 200 N; with μk = 0.30, friction = 60 N.

teach.caption: Mass is the same everywhere. Weight changes with g. Weight is never given in kilograms.

head: Force
Its partner
Third-law pair?
teach.caption: Action and reaction are equal, opposite, of the same type and act on DIFFERENT objects, so they never cancel. A book's weight and the table's support balance, but they are not a third-law pair.

teach.body: The normal force is the perpendicular push of a surface; on a level surface with no other vertical forces it equals the weight. Friction opposes sliding (or attempted sliding): f = μN, where μ has no unit. Static friction (not yet moving) has a larger maximum than kinetic friction (sliding), so starting a heavy object takes more force than keeping it moving. In the simple model friction does not depend on contact area or speed. Air resistance (drag) does grow with speed.

teach.h: A 20 kg crate (g = 10 m/s², N = 200 N)
teach.caption: Push past 90 N to start the crate; then 60 N keeps it sliding at constant velocity.

teach.h: Scenario: Luis and the linen cart
teach.body: Luis, a physical therapist assistant applicant, pushes a 50 kg linen cart. It does not budge until his push beats maximum static friction. Once it rolls, kinetic friction is 100 N. Pushing with 150 N gives F_net = 50 N and a = 50 ÷ 50 = 1.0 m/s². When he eases to exactly 100 N the forces balance: the cart keeps moving at constant velocity, not stopping. Mass stays 50 kg everywhere; its weight on Earth (g = 9.8) is 490 N.

teach.text: Action and reaction never cancel: they act on different objects. In a collision the forces are equal even when one object is much larger. Constant velocity needs zero net force. Use the net force in F = ma. Mass does not change on the Moon; weight does. Static friction's maximum is larger than kinetic friction.

items: First law: no net force means rest or constant velocity; mass measures inertia.
Second law: F_net = ma (1 N = 1 kg·m/s²); subtract friction before dividing by mass.
Third law: equal and opposite forces on different objects.
Weight W = mg in newtons; mass in kilograms is the same everywhere.
Friction f = μN; static max > kinetic; not affected by contact area in the simple model.

summary: You can now apply Newton's three laws, calculate acceleration from the net force and tell a third-law pair from a pair of balanced forces. You can also convert between mass and weight with W = mg and calculate static and kinetic friction from the normal force.

A.q: A bus brakes suddenly and a standing passenger lurches forward. Which law best explains the lurch?
A.why: The passenger's body tends to keep moving forward at the bus's old speed: inertia, Newton's first law.

whyNot.1: F = ma describes how a net force changes motion; the lurch is the body continuing its motion.
whyNot.2: The third law pairs forces on two objects; it does not explain the body carrying on forward.
whyNot.3: Gravity acts downward; the lurch is horizontal.

A.q: What is the weight on Earth of a 50 kg patient? Use g = 9.8 m/s².

whyNot.0: Gives the mass value as a force; it must be multiplied by g.
whyNot.2: Divides mass by g (50 ÷ 9.8) instead of multiplying.
whyNot.3: Weight is a force, measured in newtons, not kilograms.

A.q: A crate sits at rest on a level floor. Which statement about the forces on it is correct?
options: No forces act on the crate
Its weight exceeds the normal force
The normal force exceeds its weight
The net force on the crate is zero
A.why: At rest means no acceleration, so the forces are balanced: weight down equals normal force up, and the net force is zero.

whyNot.0: Gravity and the floor's normal force both act; they balance.
whyNot.1: A larger weight would make the crate accelerate down through the floor.
whyNot.2: A larger normal force would lift the crate upward.

B.q: A 12 kg box is pushed across a floor with a 60 N horizontal force while friction exerts 24 N. What is the box's acceleration?

whyNot.0: Uses the applied force alone (60 ÷ 12); friction must be subtracted first.
whyNot.2: Adds friction to the push (84 ÷ 12); friction opposes the motion.

B.q: A swimmer pushes backward on the water with her hands. What force moves her forward?
options: Her hands pushing back on the water
Her body's inertia carrying her on
The water pushing forward on her hands
The water's buoyant force on her body
B.why: Newton's third law: she pushes the water back, so the water pushes her forward with an equal and opposite force.

whyNot.0: That force acts on the water, not on her, so it cannot move her.
whyNot.1: Inertia keeps motion going but does not start it; a force from the water does.
whyNot.3: Buoyancy acts upward and holds her up; it does not drive her forward.

B.q: Which change would double a cart's acceleration?
options: Halving the net force on it
Doubling the net force on it
B.why: a = F_net ÷ m. Doubling the net force with the same mass doubles the acceleration.

whyNot.0: Doubling the mass halves the acceleration.
whyNot.1: Halving the force halves the acceleration.
whyNot.2: Doubling both leaves the ratio, and so the acceleration, unchanged.

C.q: A 25 kg crate is pulled across a level floor at constant velocity by a 75 N horizontal force. Using g = 10 m/s², what is the coefficient of kinetic friction? (f = μN)
C.why: Constant velocity: friction = pull = 75 N. N = mg = 25 × 10 = 250 N. μ = f ÷ N = 75 ÷ 250 = 0.30.

whyNot.1: Divides by the mass (75 ÷ 25) instead of the normal force.

C.q: An 80 kg astronaut weighs 128 N on the Moon. What is the free-fall acceleration on the Moon?

whyNot.1: 9.8 m/s² is Earth's value, not the Moon's.
whyNot.3: Subtracts mass from weight (128 − 80), which have different units.

C.q: During a collision, a 1,000 kg car accelerates at 6.0 m/s² from the force of a 2,000 kg truck. What is the truck's acceleration during the collision?
C.why: The car feels F = 1,000 × 6.0 = 6,000 N. By the third law the truck feels 6,000 N too: a = 6,000 ÷ 2,000 = 3.0 m/s².

whyNot.0: The forces are equal, not the accelerations; the larger mass accelerates less.
whyNot.2: Doubles instead of halving: twice the mass gives half the acceleration.
whyNot.3: The truck feels the same 6,000 N force, so it does accelerate.

reteach.title: The empty cart and the full cart
reteach.question: In a grocery store, why does a full cart take more effort to start, steer and stop than an empty one?

blocks.body: A full cart has more mass, so it has more inertia (first law). Push both with the same force and the full cart gets less acceleration (second law, a = F ÷ m). Whatever you push on the cart, it pushes back on your hands just as hard (third law), which is why a heavy cart 'pushes back'. A full cart also presses harder on the floor, so the wheels' friction rises with the larger normal force.

blocks.text: The cart pushes back on you with exactly the force you apply, full or empty. What differs is how much the cart accelerates.

explain.body: Inertia is resistance to a change in motion. It depends on mass alone, not on speed.

test.q: Which object has the greatest inertia?
options: A 1,000 kg car that is parked
test.why: Mass is the measure of inertia, so the 1,000 kg car has the most, even though it is not moving.

whyNot.0: Speed does not set inertia; 2 kg is a small mass.
whyNot.1: A fast baseball has little mass, so little inertia.
whyNot.3: 70 kg is less mass than the car; speed does not add inertia.

explain.body: Rearranged: a = F_net ÷ m and m = F_net ÷ a. Units: N = kg·m/s².

test.q: A net force of 36 N acts on a 9.0 kg cart. What is its acceleration?

whyNot.0: Multiplies force by mass instead of dividing.
whyNot.2: Subtracts mass from force; they have different units.

explain.body: W = mg. To find mass from weight, divide by g: m = W ÷ g. Mass is in kg, weight in N.

test.q: An object weighs 980 N on Earth. Using g = 9.8 m/s², what is its mass?

whyNot.1: Multiplies by g instead of dividing.
whyNot.2: Gives the weight value as if it were the mass.
whyNot.3: Mass is in kilograms; newtons measure force.

explain.body: f = μN. Change the surfaces (μ) or the normal force and friction changes. Contact area and sliding speed do not matter in the simple model.

test.q: In the simple friction model, which change increases the kinetic friction on a box sliding across a floor?
options: Turning it onto a larger face
Turning it onto a smaller face
test.why: More mass raises the normal force, and f = μN, so friction rises.

whyNot.0: Contact area does not change friction in the simple model.
whyNot.1: Kinetic friction does not depend on speed in the simple model.
whyNot.3: A smaller contact area does not change friction either.
